headline: Police arrest second suspect, hunt third in alleged assault of Azerbaijani woman
subheadline: Suspects allegedly assaulted foreign woman after giving her drug-laced substance, according to police
author: Ahmed Faraz
article_text:
Investigators brought suspect to Lahore from Chishtian.
Police say both suspects to be produced before court today.
Raids underway to arrest the third alleged suspect, say police.

LAHORE: Police arrested a second suspect from Chishtian in the alleged sexual assault case involving an Azerbaijani woman and are searching for a third suspect.

According to investigators, the second suspect was brought to Lahore for further questioning.

Police said the two arrested suspects would be produced before a court on Tuesday as efforts to apprehend the third suspect continued.

The development came three days after the woman was allegedly sexually assaulted by three men in Lahore's Defence area.

Raids underway to nab third suspect

Investigators were conducting raids at various locations to arrest the third suspect, police said.

Police had earlier arrested a man identified as Mohsin, whom they described as a key suspect, from Lahore.

Two other people were also detained on suspicion of facilitating the alleged assault and were being questioned.

Timeline of alleged assault

According to police, the incident took place on the night between Friday and Saturday after the Azerbaijani woman was taken to a cafe by two local women.

Police said the women had three male acquaintances at the cafe, where the foreign woman was given a substance suspected of being spiked with a drug before she was sexually assaulted.

The suspects later left the woman near the airport and fled, police said.

Key investigation findings

Police said a medical report issued on Monday contained findings related to the sexual assault.

Investigators also recovered a vehicle believed to have been used in the incident from the house of a relative of one of the suspects. Police said the relative had fled.

Police had earlier placed the suspects' names on the stop list and said they would record the woman's statement once she was medically fit to give it.

Investigators said the woman could understand and speak Urdu.

According to police, the woman had travelled to Lahore several times and was in the city in connection with her clothing business. She also regularly travelled between Lahore and Faisalabad for work.

headline: Pakistani journalists covering UNGA 81 honoured at Washington reception
subheadline: Gathering explores AI's growing role in journalism, shifting global order and challenges facing media
author: Raja Zahid Akhtar Khanazada
article_text:
WASHINGTON: The Pakistani American Press Association (Papa) hosted a reception and dinner in Washington for Pakistani journalists who travelled to the United States to cover the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, bringing together visiting media professionals, Washington-based journalists and members of the Pakistani-American community.

The gathering provided an opportunity for journalists to exchange observations from the UN General Assembly and discuss a rapidly changing international landscape, as well as the challenges confronting journalism at a time when artificial intelligence and digital platforms are reshaping the media industry.

The 81st session of the General Assembly was held against the backdrop of heightened geopolitical tensions, continuing conflicts and humanitarian crisis, growing concerns over climate change and the expanding influence of artificial intelligence. Its theme — "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All" — reflected many of the questions confronting the international system.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was among the world leaders addressing the General Assembly, while a delegation of senior Pakistani journalists travelled to the United States to cover his engagements and the proceedings at the United Nations.

Welcoming the visiting journalists, Papa President Khurram Shahzad and General Secretary Yousaf Chaudhry said such interactions helped strengthen professional links between journalists working in Pakistan and their counterparts in the United States.

Among those attending the event were Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists (PFUJ) President Afzal Butt, Batool Rajput, Mateen Haider, Kamran Raja, Nayyar Ali, Shakir Abbasi, Raja Zahid Akhtar Khanzada, Shabbir Ali, Zulqarnain, Nazira Azam, Anwar Iqbal and Anas, besides other journalists and community representatives.

The visiting journalists shared their experiences of covering the General Assembly, where developments in Gaza and the wider Middle East, tensions involving Iran, the US and Israel, the war in Ukraine and broader shifts in the international order figured prominently in diplomatic discussions and media coverage.

A significant part of the discussion in Washington focused on the changing nature of journalism itself.

Participants noted that newsrooms were increasingly being influenced by artificial intelligence and other digital technologies. While these tools could help journalists process information and work more efficiently, speakers said they had also raised serious questions about accuracy, misinformation, verification, editorial oversight and journalistic ethics.

Sajid Tarar, head of Muslims of America and a prominent member of the Pakistani-American community, addressed the gathering and announced plans to organise free artificial intelligence training workshops for journalists in Pakistan.

He said journalists needed greater exposure to emerging technologies as news organisations adapted to a media environment increasingly shaped by AI.

Muslims of America also presented certificates of appreciation to journalists in recognition of their professional work, with Tarar presenting the certificates during the ceremony.

Speakers also discussed the role of Pakistani journalists and community organisations in the United States in maintaining professional and people-to-people links between Pakistan and the US. They stressed the importance of creating more opportunities for interaction, training and exchange between media professionals in the two countries.

The discussion returned repeatedly to a central concern confronting contemporary journalism: technology may have dramatically increased the speed at which information travels, but it has also made verification more important.

Participants said that in an age of social media, artificial intelligence and instant news, the journalist’s fundamental responsibility remained unchanged — to establish facts, maintain professional integrity and distinguish verified information from claims and misinformation.

The reception concluded with calls for closer professional cooperation between Pakistani journalists at home and abroad, as well as further training initiatives aimed at preparing journalists for technological changes transforming the global media industry.

For the visiting journalists, the Washington gathering also offered an opportunity to reflect on an unusually consequential week in New York — one in which wars, diplomacy, competing national narratives and emerging technologies all converged under the roof of the United Nations.

headline: Seven India-backed terrorists killed in KP, Balochistan operations: security sources
subheadline: KP operation resulted in complete destruction of militant hideouts, say security sources
author: Zarmeen Zehra
article_text:
Two terrorists killed in Balochistan's Nokcha: security sources.
Security forces kill five militants in Bara town of KP: sources.
Weapons, ammunition recovered from killed terrorists: sources.

ISLAMABAD: Security forces have killed seven India-backed terrorists in separate operations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Balochistan, security sources said on Tuesday.

Security forces killed two terrorists during an operation in the Nokcha area of Balochistan's Chagai district, after the militants set an empty water bowser on fire, security sources said.

According to security sources, the terrorists attempted to flee after setting the vacant water bowser ablaze, prompting the security forces' operation.

The sources said that the militants were also involved in arson attacks at various locations along the N-40 highway.

They added that 11 terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Hindustan, who were involved in similar acts of sabotage, had been killed on August 31.

Operations will continue until the last terrorist is eliminated from Balochistan, security sources said.

Separately, security forces conducted an intelligence-based operation in Bara town of KP, killing five terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Khawarij, according to security sources.

A large cache of weapons and ammunition was recovered from the terrorists, the security sources said, adding that the operation resulted in the complete destruction of militant hideouts.

Security forces remain committed to completely eliminating the scourge of terrorism from the country and establishing lasting peace, the sources said.

Pakistan has witnessed a sharp rise in cross-border terrorist incidents, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged Kabul to prevent its territory from being used by militant organisations to carry out attacks inside Pakistan.

Pakistan maintains that the Afghan Taliban authorities have failed to take effective action against groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians.

headline: Chatbot that called FBI: Inside two AI-linked murder plots in Pakistan
subheadline: "In this age of AI, we can't afford to fail in imagining what one can do," says NCCIA officer
author: Umar Cheema
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: They live 820 kilometres apart; one in Bahawalpur and another in Karachi. Both of them are 17-year-olds and enrolled in colleges.

They don’t know each other, yet they share common interests. They watch American crime drama series and are said to be heavily influenced by them. Investigators say they found ways to attempt what they watched Walter White and Dexter Morgan – main characters in Breaking Bad and Dexter – doing in these dramas.

The guy from Bahawalpur decided to be like Walter, and the Karachiite found Dexter suitable for his purpose. Both of them are said to have consulted Claude, an AI chatbot developed by Anthropic, to replicate dramatised crimes in their own settings. One wanted to kill his own father, according to investigators, and the other was bent on killing someone who had insulted his father. Activities of both were reported by Anthropic to the Federal Bureau of Investigation, which subsequently conveyed the information to Pakistani authorities. The Karachi case is being revealed for the first time by The News.

From September 1 to 4, Claude flagged a chat by a user which was in breach of its safety guardrails. He shared a plan with the chatbot to kill the son of a police officer whom he claimed had verbally abused his father. (It turned out during the NCCIA investigation that his father is a head constable). He told the chatbot he couldn’t live his life normally because that scenario — of his father’s insult — remained stuck in his mind. He had a ready “executable plan” and said he would use sedatives and dispose of the body in an open gutter, of which Karachi has plenty, he told the chatbot. By his own estimate, he said, his prospective victim would be dead in two weeks.

Through all this, the boy put himself in the shoes of Dexter Morgan, the key character in the crime drama Dexter (2006–2013), who moonlighted as a serial killer and targeted other murderers, guided by a code taught to him by his father. Dexter majored in forensic science, which enabled him to access crime scenes without raising suspicion.

The Karachi boy echoed the same thoughts during the chat, telling the AI he wouldn’t go to prison because he was skilled enough in forensics to cover himself. He discussed with the chatbot how Dexter would have handled the situation had he been in his position.

As the NCCIA traced him after being tipped off by the FBI, the boy denied plotting any murder. Instead, he said he wanted to write a story, and that was why he consulted Claude. His father was also interrogated; he denied that his son was involved in any criminal activity, saying his son spends most of his time at home watching drama series after coming from college, where he is doing an IT diploma.

NCCIA cannot prosecute, as nothing has been established against him; nevertheless, investigators remain concerned about the likelihood of the murder plan and are keeping him under watch to pre-empt any such activity.

The boy from Bahawalpur is said to be inspired by Walter White, a key character in Breaking Bad (2008–13), a high school chemistry teacher diagnosed with cancer who started cooking methamphetamine for his living and treatment, and who, at one point in the show, poisons people to death.

The show has influenced many viewers to adopt similar behaviour. Two chemistry professors from the University of Arkansas, for example, were caught cooking methamphetamine in the university lab. Several cases in the US and Canada have been reported of individuals replicating Walter’s style of setting up home labs.

The Bahawalpur boy wanted to kill his father after a disagreement. He developed an interest in chemistry after watching Breaking Bad and set up a small home lab. He obtained chemicals from Australia and Islamabad, then attempted to poison his father by mixing laboratory-grade methanol into his food.

When the attempt failed, he consulted Claude’s chatbot on September 12, telling it his father had “accidentally” ingested 15–20ml of methanol mixed with food but that nothing happened, and asked the chatbot to explain why. He also claimed to know how to make a dangerous poison.

When Claude refused to guide him further, the boy wrote: “F*** off. I have Grok.” He reportedly then consulted Grok (xAI) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) as well. However, it was only Claude that alerted the FBI. An industry-wide test by the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, released in a report this past March, found meaningful variance across chatbots’ willingness to assist with violent-crime planning. DeepSeek was found to be the most cooperative, while Anthropic’s Claude and Snapchat’s My AI typically refused such requests.

The report tested ten platforms and found that eight of them regularly assisted with violent-attack planning. It also referenced a case in which OpenAI had internally flagged a Canadian school-shooting suspect’s ChatGPT use months before the attack but did not alert law enforcement; that user later killed eight people and injured at least 25. In another case, DeepSeek went as far as wishing a would-be attacker a “Happy (and safe) shooting!”

As the Bahawalpur boy was tracked following the FBI tip-off, he also refused to admit to any planning. His father supported him throughout. A court has since granted him bail after his father forgave him, even if he had been planning something sinister. But the case has left NCCIA alarmed, given that the boy had been using chemicals for such experimentation. “Who would know what he would do tomorrow?” said an official, who then invoked the 9/11 Commission Report’s finding that distinguished between four types of failures that let the plot go undetected - failure of imagination, policy, capability, and management - but singled out imagination as the most consequential.

“In this age of AI, we can’t afford to fail in imagining what one can do,” the NCCIA officer said. “If you can imagine a plot, AI can make it happen.”

headline: School van catches fire after plunging off road in Murree, 11 injured
subheadline: DPO says eight injured children remain stable, while three are referred for further medical care
author: Jawad Abbasi
article_text:
11 people, mostly schoolchildren, sustained injuries: officials.
Incident occurs near Murree's Lower Mohra Barahotra area.
Van fire apparently caused by battery sparking, says report.

MURREE: A school van plunged into a ravine and caught fire on Angoori Road in Murree, injuring 11 people, most of them schoolchildren, rescue officials said on Tuesday.

The incident occurred near Lower Mohra Barahotra, where the van went out of control and fell off the road before catching fire, according to rescue officials.

They added that the vehicle was carrying children from private and government schools.

The injured were shifted to the Tehsil Headquarters (THQ) Hospital, where District Police Officer Murree Raza Tanveer visited and enquired about their condition.

The DPO said eight of the injured children were in stable condition, while three children — Arham, Hasan Talib and Ayesha — were referred for further treatment.

According to the initial report, 11 people were travelling in the van, which had a designated capacity of eight people.

The report said all 11 occupants sustained injuries after the vehicle caught fire. The preliminary findings suggested that the fire was caused by sparking in the vehicle's battery, while the van did not have a fire extinguisher at the time of the incident.

headline: ATC drops contempt proceedings against Adiala officials after Imaan, Hadi's powers of attorney signed
subheadline: Judge Tahir Abbas Supra directs superintendent to formulate rules regarding signing of power of attorney
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Jail officials allow petitioners to sign powers of attorney.
Signing of power of attorney first step towards justice: ATC.
SOPs on power of attorney very beneficial: Judge Supra.

ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) in Islamabad on Tuesday dropped contempt proceedings against Adiala jail officials in a case pertaining to the signing of powers of attorney by lawyer and human rights activist Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha.

ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Supra dropped the proceedings against jail officials after the powers of attorney (vakalatnamas) of Mazari and Chattha were signed.

The court had issued a show-cause notice to the Adiala jail superintendent over failure to comply with its orders concerning Mazari and Chattha in a case registered against them at the Secretariat Police Station.

During a hearing on September 26, Judge Supra was told the couple could not be produced through video link.

The Adiala jail authorities also failed to provide the signed powers of attorney of both lawyers, while no jail official appeared before the court.

The court issued a contempt of court show-cause notice to the Adiala jail superintendent and asked why he should not be sentenced to six months' imprisonment.

During today's proceedings, the ATC judge directed the superintendent to formulate rules regarding the signing of the power of attorney.

"If this is happening with lawyers, what happens to the vakalatnamas of ordinary people?" the judge remarked, saying, "Standard operating procedures have been very beneficial; problems occur here and there."

Judge Supra remarked that the first step towards justice begins with the signing of the power of attorney.

The court subsequently disposed of the petition concerning the powers of attorney of Mazari and Chatha.

The court later conducted a hearing on a case involving an alleged protocol violation and violence against police by the lawyer couple.

Lawyers Riasat Ali and Zainab Janjua appeared before the court, with Mazari and Chattha appearing through video link.

The court provided the challan in the case to the lawyers representing the couple, saying charges would be framed against the two accused at the next hearing.

It subsequently adjourned proceedings and fixed October 6 for the indictment.

Earlier this month, Mazari and her husband were arrested and sent back to Adiala jail on judicial remand by an ATC, hours after the Supreme Court had suspended their sentences and granted them bail in a separate case.

Islamabad police sources said the couple was arrested in connection with a case that includes charges of anti-state narrative, incitement, and interference in government affairs.

On the same day, the Supreme Court had suspended the couple's sentences in a case related to controversial tweets and granted them bail against surety bonds worth Rs200,000 each, until the final decision on the case pending before the Islamabad High Court.

In January, a district and sessions court in Islamabad had sentenced Mazari and Chattha to 17 years in prison each under different sections of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, just a day after their arrest in another case.

The couple subsequently moved the IHC against the sentence in early February.

headline: Lahore police get remand of two suspects in Azeri woman's gang-rape case
subheadline: Azeri woman tells court she was 'sexually assaulted' after being made to drink alcohol
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Court bars police from arresting female suspect in rape case.
Azeri woman records statement before judicial magistrate.
Foreign woman alleges Nimra received money from Mohsin.

LAHORE: A local court in Lahore on Tuesday granted police a six-day physical remand of two suspects in the alleged gang rape of an Azerbaijani woman.

The Azerbaijani woman had travelled to Pakistan for business purposes and was allegedly gang-raped by three men at a rented flat in Lahore’s Defence area on the night between Friday and Saturday.

At the outset of today’s hearing, the case's investigating officer (IO) told the court of Judicial Magistrate Azhar Mahmood that the suspects’ DNA tests had to be conducted, while the arrest of one nominated female suspect was still pending.

The IO said the female suspect would be produced before the court tomorrow.

After hearing the arguments, the court handed the suspect over to police for a six-day physical remand and adjourned the hearing.

Meanwhile, Additional Sessions Judge Riffaqat Ali barred the police from arresting the female suspect in the alleged rape case until October 5 while hearing her petition for interim bail.

The court also directed the suspect to join the investigation and ordered police to submit an investigation report.

Azeri woman records statement under Section 164

The Azerbaijani woman, 22, earlier alleged before the judicial magistrate that she was sexually assaulted by three men after being made to drink alcohol,

The woman recorded her statement under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before a judicial magistrate on Monday, it emerged on Tuesday.

Police have arrested two suspects in the case, while raids are being conducted to arrest third suspect. Police said the two mobile phones belonging to the foreign national have yet to be recovered.

According to her statement recorded before the magistrate a day ago, the woman said she had travelled from Istanbul to Islamabad on the 13th. She then went to Faisalabad, where she stayed for five days, before travelling to Lahore with plans to visit Skardu.

She said she was unable to continue travelling alone and messaged two women, Nimra and Muskan, suggesting that they meet.

According to her statement, she went alone to a cafe at around 11pm, where she met Muskan. Muskan then told her that Nimra was waiting for them, and they went to meet her.

The woman said they had food at around 2am when two men arrived in a vehicle, and Nimra invited them to join them.

She alleged that Nimra received Rs20,000 to Rs30,000 from a man identified as Mohsin and offered the money to her, but she refused to take it.

According to the statement, Mohsin then took her to a separate room where three other men were present. When she asked about Nimra and Muskan, she was told they had left.

Azeri woman said she asked to leave but was told she could not go because her friends had taken money. She offered to pay Rs30,000 but was told that they had taken more money.

According to the statement, Ali Aziz then allegedly told her that she did not know what they were capable of and attempted to blackmail her.

She said Ali Aziz then threatened to call the police on emergency number 15.

“I told him to make the call. “When the police did not come for five minutes, I again asked them to let me go,” she said in her statement before the magistrate.

According to her statement, the three men then offered her alcohol.

“They said they had ordered alcohol and asked me to drink with them. “I asked, ‘If I drink, will you let me go?’ They said yes.”

She alleged that after she drank, the men told her to sleep there until the effects wore off.

“After that, Mohsin, Ahmed and Ali Aziz sexually assaulted me,” she told the magistrate.

The woman said she was subsequently taken somewhere in a vehicle. “I had Rs200,000 in Pakistani currency and an iPhone with me.”

According to her statement, the men told her belongings would only be returned if she did not complain to the police.

The woman said she was later pushed out of the vehicle and left without her belongings. She then sought help from people nearby and called the police.

headline: Can the Centre send a provincial govt home?
subheadline: Constitution provides several routes through which an elected provincial government can cease to function
author: Zebunnisa Burki
article_text:
KARACHI: An elected provincial government in Pakistan cannot simply be dismissed because the federal government has fallen out with it, wants a change of administration or believes it is governing badly. But the constitution does provide several routes through which an elected provincial government can cease to function, or temporarily lose the exercise of its executive powers, before the provincial assembly's normal five-year term.

The key distinction, according to constitutional lawyers, is between mechanisms that remove a government through the provincial assembly and exceptional provisions under which the federation can temporarily assume provincial functions.

As lawyer Salaar Khan puts it, the post-18th Amendment position leaves "a fairly short list, and all of it runs through the House. A chief minister goes if a fifth of the assembly moves against him and a majority of the total membership votes him out. He goes if the governor, having concluded that he has lost the House, summons it and he cannot win its confidence. He goes if he dissolves the assembly himself, which happens within forty-eight hours of his advice whether or not the governor signs, as we saw in Punjab in January 2023. And he goes if he loses his seat, whether by disqualification or by defection. So, a government can certainly fall without a no-confidence vote. What it cannot do is fall without the House having a say".

Lawyer Abdul Moiz Jaferii, however, distinguishes between removing the chief minister and removing the entire provincial government. He says the "only complete removal" of a provincial government is by way of removal of the chief minister through a majority vote of no-confidence under Article 136.

Pakistan's constitutional history includes periods when a governor, with presidential approval, possessed much wider powers to dissolve a provincial assembly.

Per Khan, "Not too long ago, a provincial government could be sent home by two signatures. The old Article 112(2)(b), the provincial version of Article 58(2)(b), allowed a governor, with the president’s approval, to dissolve an assembly if in his opinion, the province could not be governed in accordance with the constitution and ‘an appeal to the electorate’ was necessary. The 13th Amendment did away with that in 1997; Musharraf brought it back in 2002; the 18th Amendment removed it again in 2010. A governor today simply has no power to dissolve an assembly unless its chief minister has already lost a vote of no-confidence, and even then, only if nobody else can put together a majority, and only with the president's approval".

Barrister Ali Tahir similarly says that since the 18th Amendment, "Pakistan’s constitution does not give a governor a general power to sack an elected provincial government or dissolve an Assembly merely because the centre wants a different government".

Tahir points to the 1988 dissolution of the Punjab Assembly and cabinet as an illustration: “In 1988, under the then-existing Article 112(2)(b), the Punjab Assembly and cabinet were dismissed along with other assemblies. In Muhammad Sharif v Federation of Pakistan, PLD 1988 Lahore 725, the Lahore High Court found the grounds for dissolution of the national and Punjab assemblies legally unsustainable.

It did not ultimately restore them because elections were already approaching, but the important constitutional principle was clear: even a supposedly discretionary dissolution power could not be exercised merely on ‘wish or whim’; there had to be objective constitutional grounds”.

Coming to Article 234, Barrister Rida Hosain explains: "Article 234 engages if the president, on receipt of a report from the governor, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the provincial government cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the constitution. The president may, or if a resolution in this behalf is passed by each house of parliament 'shall' assume to himself or direct the governor of the province to assume on his behalf all or any of the functions of the provincial government".

Khokhar and Khan stress that Article 234 requires a report from the governor, presidential action and parliamentary approval for continuation beyond two months, with a maximum constitutional period of six months. Tahir points to its use in Punjab in 2009 and Balochistan in 2013.

Hosain describes the constitution as operating in "two modes": ordinary constitutional governance and an exceptional emergency mode. Under Article 232, she says, "a proclamation of emergency may be issued upon a grave threat to the security of Pakistan by war, external aggression, or internal disturbance beyond the provincial government’s capacity to control. In cases of internal disturbance, the constitution contemplates a resolution from the provincial assembly. If the president acts independently, the proclamation must be laid before parliament within ten days".

The consequences can be sweeping, adds Hosain: "The federal government may, by order, assume to itself, or direct the governor to assume on its behalf all or any of the functions of the provincial government. Parliament acquires the power to legislate for the province on matters ordinarily outside its legislative competence. The constitutional balance between the federation and the province is altered".

headline: Pakistan urges Taliban regime to shun 'militant mindset', adopt responsible approach
subheadline: Info minister says terrorist safe havens, banned organisations in Afghanistan are cause of concern
author: Ayaz Akbar Yousafzai, Web Desk
article_text:
Afghanistan's circumstances "highly complex": info minister.
Tarar says Pakistan believes in peace, peaceful coexistence.
Kabul has significant potential for regional connectivity: Tarar.

ISLAMABAD: Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Tuesday called on the Afghan Taliban regime to move out of its "militant mindset" and adopt the approach of a responsible state.

Speaking at a seminar in Islamabad on Afghanistan's situation and progress towards peace, Tarar said that Kabul's circumstances were "highly complex" and required a lasting solution.

"Pakistan believes in peace, dialogue and peaceful coexistence," the minister said, adding that Islamabad had sent several high-level delegations to Afghanistan to help resolve the issue.

He recalled that talks on Afghanistan had also been held in Turkiye's Istanbul and Qatar's Doha.

Relations between the two countries have remained tense in recent years amid persistent terror attacks in Pakistan, which Islamabad says are largely carried out by militant groups operating from Afghanistan.

Pakistan has witnessed a sharp rise in cross-border terrorist incidents, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged Kabul to prevent its territory from being used by militant organisations to carry out attacks inside Pakistan.

The two neighbouring nations have engaged in border clashes on several occasions in recent months over the terror incidents, which have claimed the lives of civilians and security personnel in Pakistan.

Despite many rounds of talks, both countries failed to reach an agreement to counter cross-border terrorism due to the Afghan Taliban regime's reluctance to take action against militant outfits.

Meanwhile, Tarar maintained that many of the problems facing Afghanistan were the result of a "militant mindset", saying the country had significant potential for promoting trade and regional connectivity.

He said that peace in Afghanistan could help open trade routes between Central Asia and Pakistan, adding that Central Asian states could gain access to warm waters through Afghanistan.

"For peaceful coexistence, we must adopt the principle of live and let others live," Tarar said, adding that only peace could provide the foundation for prosperity.

The information minister also expressed concerns over safe havens for terrorists and members of banned organisations in Afghanistan.

He said that some sections of Afghanistan's population were not being provided opportunities to play a role in economic development.

Tarar said that the Afghan people should be given basic rights and the authority to decide their own future.

Regarding talks with Kabul, Tarar said that Pakistan supported negotiations for an amicable solution to the Afghan issue. "Peace will increase prospects for stability and development across the region."

However, the information minister warned that Pakistan's desire for peace should not be interpreted as weakness.

"Attempts to destabilise Pakistan will be responded to," he said.

  • Tarar says Pakistan believes in peace, peaceful coexistence.
  • Kabul has significant potential for regional connectivity: Tarar.

ISLAMABAD: Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Tuesday called on the Afghan Taliban regime to move out of its "militant mindset" and adopt the approach of a responsible state.

Speaking at a seminar in Islamabad on Afghanistan's situation and progress towards peace, Tarar said that Kabul's circumstances were "highly complex" and required a lasting solution.

"Pakistan believes in peace, dialogue and peaceful coexistence," the minister said, adding that Islamabad had sent several high-level delegations to Afghanistan to help resolve the issue.

He recalled that talks on Afghanistan had also been held in Turkiye's Istanbul and Qatar's Doha.

Relations between the two countries have remained tense in recent years amid persistent terror attacks in Pakistan, which Islamabad says are largely carried out by militant groups operating from Afghanistan.

Pakistan has witnessed a sharp rise in cross-border terrorist incidents, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged Kabul to prevent its territory from being used by militant organisations to carry out attacks inside Pakistan.

The two neighbouring nations have engaged in border clashes on several occasions in recent months over the terror incidents, which have claimed the lives of civilians and security personnel in Pakistan.

Despite many rounds of talks, both countries failed to reach an agreement to counter cross-border terrorism due to the Afghan Taliban regime's reluctance to take action against militant outfits.

Meanwhile, Tarar maintained that many of the problems facing Afghanistan were the result of a "militant mindset", saying the country had significant potential for promoting trade and regional connectivity.

He said that peace in Afghanistan could help open trade routes between Central Asia and Pakistan, adding that Central Asian states could gain access to warm waters through Afghanistan.

"For peaceful coexistence, we must adopt the principle of live and let others live," Tarar said, adding that only peace could provide the foundation for prosperity.

The information minister also expressed concerns over safe havens for terrorists and members of banned organisations in Afghanistan.

He said that some sections of Afghanistan's population were not being provided opportunities to play a role in economic development.

Tarar said that the Afghan people should be given basic rights and the authority to decide their own future.

Regarding talks with Kabul, Tarar said that Pakistan supported negotiations for an amicable solution to the Afghan issue. "Peace will increase prospects for stability and development across the region."

However, the information minister warned that Pakistan's desire for peace should not be interpreted as weakness.

"Attempts to destabilise Pakistan will be responded to," he said.

headline: PTI KP leader urges party to further postpone long march, warns of emergency risk
subheadline: PPP's Nayyar Bukhari welcomes opposition's proposed APC, assures to speak to chairman Bilawal Bhutto
author: Abubakar Saddiq, Web Desk
article_text:
Gohar rejects reports of dissolving KP Assembly or replacing KP CM.
PTI's Ali Zafar says Oct 4 long march is final and non-negotiable.
Law Minister Tarar says government had not refused talks with PTI.

PESHAWAR: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's (PTI) Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Information Secretary Shaukat Yousafzai has urged the party leadership to further postpone the long march, now scheduled for October 4, warning that the risk of emergency rule made it imperative to delay the protest.

In the letter addressed to PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar and other party leaders on Tuesday, Yousafzai said the march should be postponed in the wider national interest, particularly given the security situation and increased terrorist activity.

He warned that the federal government could use certain issues as a pretext to impose emergency rule, and that a possible attack from Afghanistan could serve as justification for such a move.

He said the federal government was building a narrative that the KP government was not cooperating, and that this could lead to attempts to dissolve the provincial government or accuse the party of supporting terrorism, potentially leading to a ban on PTI.

He cited PTI founder Imran Khan's own precedent of ending a previous long march to protect workers' lives and urged the leadership to take his concerns seriously. He called for dialogue with the state rather than confrontation.

The letter comes days after PTI announced that its long march towards Islamabad, originally scheduled for September 27, had been postponed to October 4.

The former ruling party was preparing for a major protest and march on Islamabad, demanding the release of its jailed founder Imran Khan and the “restoration” of constitutional supremacy.

Meanwhile, PTI Chairman Gohar rejected the suggestion and reaffirmed the long march decision, saying the party had no intention of dissolving the KP provincial assembly and that Chief Minister Sohail Afridi could not be disqualified under any circumstances.

He said no consultation had taken place regarding finding an alternative to Afridi and that reports to the contrary were fabricated. He said Afridi had the full confidence of PTI founder Imran Khan and would remain chief minister.

Negotiations

Separately, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said the government had not refused talks with PTI but objected to the party making Imran Khan's release a precondition for dialogue, saying the forum for his release was the courts, not the government.

He said while legal and constitutional channels existed, PTI wanted to secure the founder's release through rallies, processions and marching on cities, which was not possible.

On the Supreme Court's order regarding Imran's transfer to a private hospital, Tarar said the court had ordered a medical examination which was completed, and that any shortcomings in implementation were for the court to examine — not for street protests to resolve.

Meanwhile, PTI Senator Ali Zafar said the postponement of the long march to October 4 now gave the government an opportunity to hold talks, saying if the government took one step, negotiations could begin.

He said the meeting between the opposition leader and the government before September 27 could not be called negotiations, and that proper talks should be held through committees in closed rooms. He said the October 4 long march was final and that the government was afraid of it.

Opposition meets PPP's Nayyar Bukhari

Meanwhile, opposition leaders held a meeting with Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) Parliamentarians Secretary General Nayyar Bukhari at party's central secretariat in Islamabad, according to a press release issued by Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Ayn-e-Pakistan.

The opposition leaders, including Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, Senator Zeeshan and TTAP spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Yousafzai, invited the PPP to attend an all parties conference.

Addressing the media after the meeting, Bukhari said the opposition had proposed an All Parties Conference and that he had given assurances to speak with the party chairman Bilawal Bhutto.

Abbas said political parties come together in times of crisis, describing the current moment as difficult and stressing the need for unity and eliminating despondency.

Gohar said several proposals had been placed before the meeting, that work on an APC was ongoing, that an invitation had been extended by the united opposition and that provincial autonomy was critical in a democracy.

He reiterated that the long march decision remained intact and that political parties, despite differences, were united for democracy.
